Week 8: Maps and Geospatial Analysis in R

Join your data to the real chiefdom boundaries, then colour, classify, layer and save it

Students work through the cards in order. Lecturers see every card from the start.

One skill: putting data on a map. Every map on these cards carries a number, a case count, a positivity rate, a class, because a map of boundaries alone tells a reader nothing.

Six cards, five worked maps and five exercises each. All 208 chiefdoms come from the real national boundary file, and every figure comes from the same dummy dataset you have used since Week 1.

From a shapefile to a ready to map layer

Read the boundaries, check the CRS, and join your data on the code

This browser has no speech engine. Chrome or Edge will read the card aloud.

When to do this

At the start of any mapping job. Ten minutes here saves an afternoon: the wrong CRS or a join on names produces a map that looks plausible and is wrong.

How it goes together

st_read() to load, st_crs() to check, then left_join() with the boundaries on the left so the geometry survives. Aggregate your cases to one row per chiefdom first.

What happensillustration

A map is a table with a geometry column

Everything you learned in Modules 1 to 6 still applies. st_read() gives you a data frame; it simply has one extra column, geometry, holding the shape of each row. filter(), select(), mutate() and left_join() all work on it, and the geometry travels along.

The map is the easy half

Two things go wrong far more often than the plotting code: the join and the coordinate system. Join on a code, never a name, two chiefdoms here are both called KOYA. And check the CRS before you plot, because two layers in different systems will not line up no matter how good the code looks.

What this module does not do

No boundary only maps. Drawing the outlines is one line and tells you nothing; every map here carries data: a count, a rate, a class: and the work is choosing the colour, the classes and the layers so the reader sees the pattern rather than the prettiness.

1Read the boundaries

library(pacman) p_load(readr, dplyr, sf, ggplot2) bounds <- st_read("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")
R Consoleoutput
Reading layer `chiefdoms_sl' from data source `chiefdoms_sl.geojson' using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 208 features and 7 fields
Geometry type: POLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -13.3074 ymin: 6.9234 xmax: -10.2706 ymax: 10.0099
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
Explanation
  • 208 features and 7 fields means 208 chiefdoms, seven ordinary columns and the geometry column on top.
  • The bounding box is a sanity check: longitude around -13 to -10 and latitude 7 to 10 is Sierra Leone. Values in the hundreds of thousands would mean a projected CRS in metres.
  • st_read("chiefdoms_sl.shp") reads the shapefile version: same result, four files instead of one.

2Check the CRS and the field names

st_crs(bounds)$input names(bounds)
R Consoleoutput
[1] "WGS 84"

[1] "CCODE"      "FIRST_REGI" "FIRST_RE_1" "FIRST_DNAM"
[5] "FIRST_DCOD" "FIRST_CHIE" "adm3"       "geometry"
Explanation
  • WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) is degrees of latitude and longitude, what GPS and DHIS2 use, so most malaria data is already in it.
  • A CRS of NA is the usual reason a map comes out blank or two layers refuse to overlay. For a shapefile that means the .prj file went missing.
  • The field names come from whoever built the file: district is FIRST_DNAM, chiefdom is FIRST_CHIE, and the chiefdom code is CCODE.

3Aggregate the cases to one row per chiefdom

cases <- read_csv("routine_cases_dummy.csv") chief_totals <- cases %>% distinct() %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE)) nrow(chief_totals) range(chief_totals$confirmed)
R Consoleoutput
[1] 208
[1] 113 797
Explanation
  • A map needs one number per shape, so the summarising comes first, 1,248 records collapse to 208 rows.
  • distinct() removes the duplicated record; leaving it in would inflate one chiefdom by a month of cases.
  • 113 to 797 confirmed cases is the range the colour scale will have to cover.

4Join on the code, with the boundaries on the left

map_data <- bounds %>% mutate(chiefdom_code = as.numeric(CCODE)) %>% left_join(chief_totals, by = "chiefdom_code") c(features = nrow(map_data), missing = sum(is.na(map_data$confirmed))) class(map_data)
R Consoleoutput
features  missing
     208        0

[1] "sf"         "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
Explanation
  • Boundaries on the left keeps the sf class and the geometry. Join the other way round and you get a plain data frame with the shapes gone.
  • Zero missing values is the check that matters. Any number above zero means chiefdoms that will be blank on the map.
  • Joining on chiefdom_code rather than the name avoids the two KOYA chiefdoms and every case and spelling difference between systems.

5The quickest possible look

plot(map_data["confirmed"])
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • plot() on a single column of an sf object gives you a coloured map in one line, which is all you want at this stage.
  • The quotes matter: map_data["confirmed"] keeps the geometry, map_data$confirmed is a bare vector and plots a scatter of nothing useful.
  • Everything after this card is ggplot(), because plot() gives you no control over colour, classes, layers or labels.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

st_read("file.geojson")Boundaries in, as a data frame plus geometry
st_crs(bounds)$inputCheck the coordinate system before anything else
group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise()One number per shape, before any plotting
left_join(bounds, totals, by = "chiefdom_code")Boundaries on the left; join on the code
plot(map_data["confirmed"])A one line look, with no control

What people writeWhat it should beWhy
1bounds <- readOGR("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")bounds <- st_read("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")readOGR() is from the retired rgdal package. sf replaces it with st_read().
2bounds <- st_read(chiefdoms_sl.geojson)bounds <- st_read("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")A file name is text, so it needs quotes. Without them R looks for an object with that name and errors.
3chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.remove = TRUE))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))The argument is na.rm. R will not match a name it does not know and errors.
4st_read("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")bounds <- st_read("chiefdoms_sl.geojson")Without the arrow the answer is printed and thrown away. Nothing is stored, so the next line has nothing to work with.
5chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = "TRUE"))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))TRUE and FALSE are logical values, not text, no quotes.
6chief_totals <- cases %> group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))The pipe is three characters: %>%. Anything else is a syntax error.
7chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))This column has a missing value, so without na.rm = TRUE the whole calculation comes back as NA.
8chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = T))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))T is only a shortcut, and it can be overwritten, somebody writing T <- 0 earlier in the script breaks your code silently. Write TRUE.
9chief_totals <- cases %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))Without group_by() the summary collapses the whole table to one row instead of one row per group.
10chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))chief_totals <- cases %>% group_by(chiefdom_code) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE))Name the result inside summarise(), or the new column is called something like sum(confirmed) and every later line has to quote it in backticks.

Step 1 of 5  /  geom_sf

The first map in ggplot

One geom, one aesthetic, and the map is a plot like any other

When to use it

As soon as the join is clean. From here on the map is a ggplot, so everything you know about labs(), themes and facets applies unchanged.

How to use it

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf() draws the shapes. Put a column in aes(fill = ) and the shapes are coloured by it. theme_void() removes the graticule and axes that no reader needs.

What happensillustration

1The shapes, with no data

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • geom_sf() reads the geometry column on its own, you never name x and y.
  • This is the boundary only map, and it is where most beginners stop. It carries no information at all beyond the shape of the country.
  • Useful for one thing: proving the layer loaded and the CRS is sane before you add data.

2Colour the shapes by a column

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed))
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • fill goes inside aes() because it depends on a column. A fixed colour goes outside: geom_sf(fill = "grey80").
  • This is a choropleth, and the default ggplot2 gradient runs dark for low and light for high, the opposite of what most readers expect, which is why the next card exists.
  • The legend appears automatically, labelled with the column name.

3Drop the axes nobody needs

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed)) + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • theme_void() strips the panel, grid and axis text. Latitude and longitude labels help nobody reading a district report.
  • theme_minimal() keeps a faint graticule if you do want coordinates.
  • The map itself is unchanged: a theme only ever changes the furniture.

4Thin white borders, so 208 shapes stay readable

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • colour is the border and fill is the inside. Mixing them up is the commonest ggplot2 mistake with polygons.
  • At 208 shapes, thick borders swallow the small chiefdoms. 0.1 is about right for a page width map; drop to 0 for a thumbnail.
  • linewidth replaced size for lines in ggplot2 3.4. Old code using size still runs but warns.

5Fixing the coordinates in place

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + coord_sf(expand = FALSE) + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • coord_sf() is added automatically, but naming it lets you control it: expand = FALSE removes the white margin around the country.
  • It also holds the aspect ratio, so Sierra Leone is never stretched sideways by a wide plotting window.
  • coord_sf(crs = 4326) reprojects on the fly for display only, without touching the data, useful when one layer arrives in a different system.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf()The shapes, no data
geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed))A choropleth: colour by a column
geom_sf(fill = "grey80")A fixed colour goes outside aes()
colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1Borders: colour is the edge, fill is the inside
theme_void() / coord_sf(expand = FALSE)Remove the furniture; fix the aspect and padding

Choosing the colours

The scale decides what the reader sees, the same data can look flat or alarming

Read aloud ready

The voice reads the headings, the when and how boxes, the explanations and the recap, and marks each sentence with an arrow as it goes. Code is skipped on purpose: read it on screen while you listen.

This browser has no speech engine. Chrome or Edge will read the card aloud.

When to use it

Every map you will show anybody. The default gradient is hard to read, unfriendly to colour blind readers and prints badly in grey. Changing it is one line.

How to use it

scale_fill_viridis_c() for counts, scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) for a familiar sequential ramp, scale_fill_gradient2() when there is a meaningful middle, and na.value for the shapes with no data.

What happensillustration

1Viridis, the safe default for counts

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Viridis is perceptually even, so equal steps in the data look like equal steps in colour, the default gradient does not manage that.
  • It stays readable printed in black and white, and for the commonest forms of colour blindness.
  • _c is for a continuous column. scale_fill_viridis_d() is the discrete version, for classes, which is the next card.

2A sequential ColorBrewer ramp

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • ColorBrewer palettes were designed for maps, and "Blues", "Greens", "Reds" and "YlOrRd" are the sequential ones you will use most.
  • direction = 1 matters: by default scale_fill_distiller() reverses the palette, giving you dark for low cases, which nobody reads correctly.
  • Dark equals more is the convention. Break it and half your audience will read the map backwards.

3A diverging scale, for a rate with a meaningful middle

map_data <- map_data %>% mutate(tpr = confirmed / tested * 100) ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = tpr), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#4575b4", mid = "#ffffbf", high = "#d73027", midpoint = 46, name = "Test positivity (%)") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Use a diverging scale only when the middle means something, a national average, a target, a change of zero. For plain counts it invents a story.
  • midpoint is the value that gets the middle colour. Leave it at the default 0 with a rate and every chiefdom comes out red.
  • This map answers a different question from the count map: where testing finds malaria most often, rather than where the most cases are.

4The chiefdoms with no data

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90", name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • na.value is the colour for shapes your join did not match. The default is a mid grey that readers often mistake for a data value.
  • Grey is right and zero is wrong. A facility that did not report has not reported zero cases, and colouring it as zero understates the map.
  • Say it in the caption too: "grey chiefdoms did not report". A map with silent gaps is a map that misleads.

5Reversing, and the warm palettes

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1, name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Warm palettes carry meaning: red says problem. That is useful for case burden and wrong for something neutral like population.
  • scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1) flips any viridis option if you want bright for low.
  • Pick the palette once for a whole report and keep it. Readers learn a colour scheme, then get confused when the next page changes it.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

scale_fill_viridis_c()Even steps, colour blind safe, prints in grey
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1)ColorBrewer ramp; direction = 1 puts dark at the top
scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 46)Diverging, for a rate with a meaningful middle
na.value = "grey90"Shapes with no data: grey, never zero
option = "magma" / direction = -1Other viridis options; flip the direction

Step 3 of 5  /  cut fermenter brewer

Classes instead of a smooth ramp

Four groups a reader can name beat a gradient nobody can decode

Locked. Get all five exercises in the previous card correct and this one opens.

Mohamed Sillah Kanu
AI Assistant Tutor

Press start and I will take you through this card.
Lecture mode ready

Press start and the card teaches itself: it dims everything except the part being discussed, points at it, writes each code block out, then walks the code line by line explaining what each line does. It stops at the exercises and hands over to you. Voice and speed are set in the Read aloud panel below.

Read aloud ready

The voice reads the headings, the when and how boxes, the explanations and the recap, and marks each sentence with an arrow as it goes. Code is skipped on purpose: read it on screen while you listen.

This browser has no speech engine. Chrome or Edge will read the card aloud.

When to use it

Whenever the map goes into a report or onto a wall. A reader cannot tell 480 from 520 on a gradient, but "400 to 600" is a group they can find in a table and act on.

How to use it

cut() or ntile() to make the classes, then scale_fill_brewer() for the discrete colours. scale_fill_fermenter() bins a continuous column for you in one line.

What happensillustration

1Quartiles, with ntile()

map_data <- map_data %>% mutate(class = ntile(confirmed, 4), class = factor(class, labels = c("Lowest 25%", "25-50%", "50-75%", "Highest 25%"))) count(st_drop_geometry(map_data), class)
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • ntile(confirmed, 4) splits the 208 chiefdoms into four equal groups of 52, quartiles by count of areas, not by case numbers.
  • Equal sized groups always fill the map evenly, which is honest about ranking and silent about magnitude: the top group might be twice the third or twenty times it.
  • st_drop_geometry() before count(), or dplyr drags 208 polygons through the summary.

2Discrete colours for discrete classes

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Case burden") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • scale_fill_brewer() is the discrete twin of scale_fill_distiller(). Feed it a factor and it hands out one colour per level.
  • The legend becomes four labelled boxes, which is what makes the map readable across a room.
  • If the legend order comes out wrong, fix the factor levels, the scale follows the factor, not the other way round.

3Breaks you choose yourself

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_fermenter(breaks = c(200, 400, 600), palette = "Greens", direction = 1, name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • scale_fill_fermenter() bins a continuous column as it draws, so you skip the mutate() entirely.
  • Round breaks beat computed ones for a report: 200, 400, 600 are numbers people repeat back to you; 302.4 is not.
  • Choosing breaks is a decision, not a detail. Move them and the same data tells a different story, so state them in the caption.

4Equal intervals against quantiles

# equal intervals: same width, uneven counts map_data %>% mutate(eq = cut(confirmed, breaks = 4)) %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(eq)
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • cut(x, breaks = 4) divides the range into four equal widths, so the number of chiefdoms per class is whatever the data gives, here 54, 85, 54 and 15.
  • Equal intervals show magnitude honestly: the top class really is the high burden group. Quantiles show rank and always look balanced.
  • Neither is right in general. Say which you used, because a reader cannot tell from the map.

5The same data, smooth and classed, side by side

# a gradient hides the groups; classes hide the fine detail p1 <- ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed)) + scale_fill_viridis_c() + theme_void() p2 <- ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = class)) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") + theme_void() p_load(patchwork) p1 + p2
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • patchwork puts two finished plots side by side with a plus sign, the fastest way to compare two treatments of the same data.
  • Continuous is right for exploring, where you want every difference visible. Classes are right for reporting, where you want a reader to act.
  • Make this comparison once for each indicator and keep the winner. Do not print both in the same report.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

ntile(confirmed, 4)Four equal sized groups: quartiles by area
cut(confirmed, breaks = 4)Four equal width bands: uneven counts
scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues")Discrete colours for a factor
scale_fill_fermenter(breaks = c(200, 400, 600))Bin a continuous column as you draw
st_drop_geometry() %>% count(class)Check the class sizes before you trust the map

Overlaying layers

Chiefdom fill, district outline, facility points, labels, in that order

Press start and I will take you through this card.
Lecture mode ready

Press start and the card teaches itself: it dims everything except the part being discussed, points at it, writes each code block out, then walks the code line by line explaining what each line does. It stops at the exercises and hands over to you. Voice and speed are set in the Read aloud panel below.

Read aloud ready

The voice reads the headings, the when and how boxes, the explanations and the recap, and marks each sentence with an arrow as it goes. Code is skipped on purpose: read it on screen while you listen.

This browser has no speech engine. Chrome or Edge will read the card aloud.

When to use it

Whenever one layer is not enough: chiefdom colours under district boundaries, health facilities on top of a burden map, or names on the areas a reader needs to find.

How to use it

Add one geom_sf() per layer, each with its own data =. They draw in the order you write them, so the fill goes first and the outlines and points go after. fill = NA makes a layer show only its borders.

What happensillustration

1A second layer for the district boundaries

districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry)) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • st_union() inside summarise() dissolves the chiefdoms of each district into one shape, this is the standard way to get a district layer from a chiefdom file.
  • fill = NA is what makes the second layer an outline instead of a solid block that hides your data.
  • With two layers, ggplot() takes no data and each geom_sf() names its own data =.

2Facilities as points on top

facilities <- cases %>% distinct(chiefdom_code, facility, lon, lat) %>% st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + geom_sf(data = facilities, colour = "red", size = 1.4, alpha = 0.8) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) is how a plain table of GPS readings becomes a map layer. Longitude first, latitude second, swapping them puts Sierra Leone in the Indian Ocean.
  • crs = 4326 tells sf the numbers are degrees. Without it the points have no CRS and will not overlay.
  • Points go after the polygons, or the fill paints over them.

3Sizing the points by a value

ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, fill = "grey92", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + geom_sf(data = facilities, aes(size = confirmed), colour = "#d73027", alpha = 0.6) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.5, 6), name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • A graduated symbol map avoids the trap of choropleths, where a big rural chiefdom looks more important than a small busy town.
  • size inside aes() maps the value; scale_size_continuous(range) controls how big the smallest and largest circles get.
  • Keep the base plain when the points carry the data. Two variables fighting on one map is one too many.

4Labels, only where they help

top3 <- map_data %>% slice_max(confirmed, n = 3) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + geom_sf_text(data = top3, aes(label = FIRST_CHIE), size = 3, colour = "white") + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • geom_sf_text() puts a label at each centroid; geom_sf_label() adds a box behind it for busy backgrounds.
  • Label the few shapes the reader must find. Labelling all 208 chiefdoms produces a grey smudge.
  • slice_max() from Week 5 picks the three worth naming; the label layer takes only that small table.

5Highlighting one district in context

bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM == "BO") ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, fill = "grey93", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + geom_sf(data = bo, aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Two layers of the same file: everything in grey, then the filtered subset in colour on top.
  • Better than cropping to Bo, because the reader still sees where in the country it is.
  • To crop as well, add coord_sf(xlim = , ylim = ), but keep a small inset of the whole country if you do.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

geom_sf(data = x) + geom_sf(data = y)One geom per layer, drawn in the order written
st_union(geometry) in summarise()Dissolve chiefdoms into district outlines
fill = NA, colour = "black"An outline layer that does not hide the fill
st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)Coordinate columns into a point layer
geom_sf_text(aes(label = ...))Labels at the centroids: for a few shapes only

What people writeWhat it should beWhy
1districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% aggregate(geometry = st_union(geometry))districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))aggregate() is the base R way and returns a different shape. The dplyr verb is summarise().
2bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))Without the arrow the answer is printed and thrown away. Nothing is stored, so the next line has nothing to work with.
3districts <- bounds %> group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))The pipe is three characters: %>%. Anything else is a syntax error.
4bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM = "BO")bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM == "BO")One equals sign assigns; two compare. Inside filter() a single = is read as naming an argument, and R errors.
5bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM == BO)bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM == "BO")A value in a column is text, so it needs quotes. Without them R looks for an object with that name, object not found.
6top3 <- map_data %>% slice_max(confirmed, 3)top3 <- map_data %>% slice_max(confirmed, n = 3)In slice_max() the count has to be named: n = 3. Unnamed, it is taken as the column to rank by.
7districts <- bounds %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))Without group_by() the summary collapses the whole table to one row instead of one row per group.
8districts <- bounds %>% Group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))districts <- bounds %>% group_by(FIRST_DNAM) %>% summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry))R is case sensitive: Group_by() does not exist. It is group_by(), all lower case.
9ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = confirmed)) + geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, colour = "black") + theme_void(ggplot() + geom_sf(data = map_data, aes(fill = confirmed)) + geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, colour = "black") + theme_void()A bracket is missing. R waits for the rest of the line and shows a + prompt instead of an answer: count the brackets.
10bo <- map_data %>% subset(FIRST_DNAM == "BO")bo <- map_data %>% filter(FIRST_DNAM == "BO")subset() is base R and behaves differently inside functions. The dplyr verb is filter().

Finishing the map and getting it out

Titles, a legend that fits, two maps side by side, and a file you can send

This browser has no speech engine. Chrome or Edge will read the card aloud.

When to use it

The last twenty minutes before a map goes into a bulletin, and the moment somebody asks for "the map as a picture" or "the layer so I can open it in QGIS".

How to use it

labs() for the words, theme() for the legend, facet_wrap() for one map per period, ggsave() for a PNG and st_write() when the layer itself has to travel.

What happensillustration

1The words that make a map usable

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed\ncases") + labs(title = "Confirmed malaria cases by chiefdom", subtitle = "January to June 2026", caption = "Source: routine facility reports. Grey: no report received.") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • A map with no period and no source is unusable six months later, and undefendable in a meeting.
  • The legend name is the one label a reader must have: "Confirmed cases", not the column name confirmed.
  • \n inside the name wraps the legend title so a long one does not stretch the map.

2Moving the legend so the map gets the space

ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"))
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Sierra Leone is taller than it is wide, so a legend on the right wastes page width. Bottom or "inside" suits a portrait country.
  • theme() comes after theme_void(), or the void resets your changes.
  • legend.position = "none" drops the legend entirely, which is right when the classes are already named in the caption.

3One map per period

by_quarter <- cases %>% distinct() %>% mutate(quarter = if_else(month %in% c("January","February","March"), "Q1", "Q2")) %>% group_by(chiefdom_code, quarter) %>% summarise(confirmed = sum(confirmed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") quarter_map <- bounds %>% mutate(chiefdom_code = as.numeric(CCODE)) %>% left_join(by_quarter, by = "chiefdom_code") ggplot(quarter_map) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) + facet_wrap(~ quarter) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • Faceting a map needs one row per shape per panel, so the join happens after the quarter summary, 416 rows for 208 chiefdoms in two quarters.
  • Both panels share one colour scale, which is the whole point: the same colour means the same number in both, so the growth from Q1 to Q2 is visible.
  • Give facets fewer than about six panels. Twelve monthly maps on one page are too small to read.

4A rate map, next to the count map

rate_map <- map_data %>% mutate(tpr = confirmed / tested * 100) ggplot(rate_map) + geom_sf(aes(fill = tpr), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1, name = "Positivity (%)") + labs(title = "Test positivity by chiefdom", subtitle = "Confirmed as a share of those tested, January to June 2026") + theme_void()
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • A count map shows where the cases are; a rate map shows where testing finds malaria most often. They rarely have the same pattern, and confusing them misdirects supplies.
  • Always compute the rate from the two totals inside the chiefdom summary, never by averaging facility rates.
  • Say which one a map shows in the title. "Malaria map" on a slide has started more arguments than any other caption.

5Saving the picture, and the layer

p <- ggplot(map_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = confirmed), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Confirmed") + theme_void() ggsave("chiefdom_cases.png", plot = p, width = 7, height = 8, dpi = 300) # and the layer itself, for QGIS or a colleague st_write(map_data, "chiefdom_cases.geojson", delete_dsn = TRUE)
Plots panemap
Explanation
  • ggsave() saves the last plot, or the one you name. Set width and height in inches: 300 dpi is print quality, 150 is plenty for a slide.
  • Match the shape of the file to the shape of the country. A 10 x 6 landscape PNG of Sierra Leone is mostly white space.
  • st_write() writes the joined layer out: .geojson for sharing, .shp when the recipient insists. delete_dsn = TRUE overwrites an existing file instead of erroring.

Recap of this card

Read this through once, then work the five exercises below without scrolling back up.

labs(title, subtitle, caption)Period and source, or the map is undefendable
scale_fill_*(name = "Confirmed cases")The legend title the reader needs
theme(legend.position = "bottom")A portrait country wants the legend below
facet_wrap(~ quarter)One panel per period, sharing one colour scale
ggsave() / st_write()The picture, and the layer itself
